_about: Queue of guides for the weekly auto-draft system (scripts/draft-guide.mjs). The first topic in 'queue' whose guide doesn't exist yet (and has no open draft) is written next. Facts here are checked by hand; the AI may only use these numbers (plus the site's appliance data and simple arithmetic). Add new topics at the end. Finished topics move to 'done'.

queue.keyword: how to store a portable power station
queue.question: How should I store a portable power station between power outages so it is ready and the battery lasts?
queue.angle: A practical storage checklist for people who keep a power station for emergencies.
facts: Store it partly charged — often around 50–80% — unless the manual says otherwise.
Top it up every 3–6 months; all batteries slowly lose charge while stored.
Keep it in a cool, dry place out of direct sun; avoid hot cars and damp garages.
Most lithium batteries should not be charged below 32°F (0°C) unless they have built-in heating; capacity also drops in the cold.
LiFePO4 power stations are commonly rated for about 3,000–4,000 cycles; NMC units about 500–1,000 cycles.
Charge it fully and test it before storm season by running a lamp or fan from it.
Keep cables, adapters and the manual stored with it.

queue.keyword: power station to run a window AC
queue.question: Can a portable power station run a window air conditioner, and for how long?
queue.angle: Honest answer: possible with a big unit, but short runtimes; better cooling options for outages.
facts: A typical 8,000 BTU window AC draws about 700 W running and about 1,800 W for a moment when the compressor starts.
The compressor cycles; it runs roughly 60% of the time on a hot day.
Runtime ≈ capacity × 0.85 ÷ watts. At a steady 700 W: 1,000 Wh ≈ 1.2 hours, 2,000 Wh ≈ 2.4 hours, 3,600 Wh ≈ 4.4 hours.
With the compressor cycling about 60% of the time (average about 420 W): 1,000 Wh ≈ 2 hours, 2,000 Wh ≈ 4 hours, 3,600 Wh ≈ 7.3 hours.
The power station's surge rating must exceed about 1,800 W and its continuous output must exceed about 700 W.
A box fan uses about 75 W and a ceiling fan about 60 W — roughly a tenth of a window AC.
Central air conditioners run on 240 V and cannot be run by most portable power stations.
Cooling tips: cool one small room, close blinds, run the AC on a higher temperature setting, use fans, add solar during the day.

queue.keyword: power station for a chest freezer
queue.question: What size power station do I need to run a chest freezer during a power outage?
queue.angle: Chest freezers are one of the most battery-friendly big appliances; show sizing and how long food stays frozen.
facts: A typical chest freezer draws about 100 W while running and about 800 W for a moment when the compressor starts.
The compressor runs roughly 40% of the time, so daily use is about 100 × 24 × 0.4 = 960 Wh.
Sizing: 960 Wh ÷ 0.85 × 1.2 ≈ 1,400 Wh for one day.
Runtime at an average of about 40 W: 1,000 Wh ≈ 21 hours, 2,000 Wh ≈ 42 hours, 3,600 Wh ≈ 76 hours.
USDA guidance: a full freezer holds its temperature about 48 hours (about 24 hours if half full) if the door stays closed.
Chest freezers lose less cold air when opened than upright freezers because cold air sinks.
Tips: keep it full (add jugs of water), keep the lid closed, run it in bursts while checking temperature with a thermometer, keep it in a cool place.

queue.question: How long will a portable power station run or charge a laptop?
queue.angle: Remote work during outages and travel; why USB-C is more efficient than the AC outlet.
facts: A typical laptop uses about 60 W while working; a desktop PC with monitor about 250 W.
Runtime from the AC outlet ≈ capacity × 0.85 ÷ watts. At 60 W: 300 Wh ≈ 4 hours, 500 Wh ≈ 7 hours, 1,000 Wh ≈ 14 hours.
Charging over USB-C Power Delivery skips the inverter and is more efficient (about 90%): 500 Wh ≈ 7.5 hours at 60 W.
Check the USB-C port's wattage (for example 60 W or 100 W) is at least your laptop charger's rating.
A Wi-Fi router and modem uses about 20 W; add it to your total if you need internet.
Switch off the AC inverter when not needed — it uses power even with nothing plugged in.
US airlines commonly allow lithium batteries up to 100 Wh in carry-on without approval; most power stations are larger — check the airline's rules.

queue.keyword: power station for an electric blanket
queue.question: How long will a power station run an electric blanket or heated mattress pad?
queue.angle: The most battery-friendly way to stay warm in a winter outage or cold camping night.
facts: Electric blankets and heated mattress pads typically use about 50–100 W.
A 100 W blanket for 8 hours uses about 800 Wh; a 50 W blanket about 400 Wh.
Runtime ≈ capacity × 0.85 ÷ watts. At 100 W: 500 Wh ≈ 4 hours, 1,000 Wh ≈ 8.5 hours, 2,000 Wh ≈ 17 hours. At 50 W: double those times.
Most blankets have heat settings and timers; lower settings and pre-warming the bed then switching to low stretch the battery.
A 1,500 W space heater drains a 1,000 Wh power station in about 34 minutes — roughly 15 times faster than a 100 W blanket.
Safety: follow the blanket's instructions, don't fold or bunch it while on, and don't use damaged blankets.
Some 12 V heated blankets can run from the power station's 12 V port, which is more efficient than AC.

queue.keyword: power station to run a coffee maker
queue.question: Can a portable power station run a coffee maker, and how much battery does it use?
queue.angle: Morning coffee during an outage or at camp: output matters more than capacity.
facts: A drip coffee maker uses about 900 W while brewing; an electric kettle about 1,500 W.
A 12-minute brew at 900 W uses about 180 Wh, or about 210 Wh from the battery after inverter loss.
Boiling a kettle for about 6 minutes at 1,500 W uses about 150 Wh, or about 175 Wh from the battery.
The power station's continuous output must be above the appliance's watts with headroom: about 1,100 W or more for a 900 W coffee maker, about 1,800 W for a 1,500 W kettle.
Keeping the coffee maker's hot plate on keeps drawing power; pour the coffee into a thermos instead.
Manual options (pour-over with kettle-boiled water, French press) use only the kettle's energy.
Avoid running the coffee maker at the same moment a fridge compressor starts if the power station is near its output limit.

queue.keyword: how long to charge a power station
queue.question: How long does it take to charge a portable power station from the wall, a car or solar?
queue.angle: Simple formula and examples for each charging method.
facts: Charging time ≈ energy to add (Wh) ÷ charging input (W) ÷ about 0.9 for charging losses.
Example from the wall: adding 1,000 Wh at 500 W of AC input ≈ 2.2 hours; at 1,000 W ≈ 1.1 hours. Many units slow down near 100%.
Car 12 V sockets typically supply about 100–120 W: adding 1,000 Wh takes roughly 9–11 hours of driving (1,000 ÷ 120 ÷ 0.9 ≈ 9.3; 1,000 ÷ 100 ÷ 0.9 ≈ 11.1).
Solar: real panel output is about 75% of the rating; a 200 W panel in 5 good sun hours adds about 675–750 Wh a day.
The power station's maximum AC and solar input ratings (in watts) are on the spec sheet and set the fastest possible charge.
Charging from 20% to 80% is faster than 0–100% because charging slows at the top.
Don't charge most lithium batteries below 32°F (0°C) unless the unit has battery heating.

queue.question: Can a portable power station back up my home during a power outage, and what can it realistically run?
queue.angle: What a portable power station can and can't do for home backup; essentials-first planning.
facts: Essentials and typical figures: full-size fridge about 1,100–1,900 Wh a day; Wi-Fi router about 20 W (480 Wh a day); LED bulb about 10 W; phone charging about 15 W; CPAP about 30–60 W without humidifier; sump pump (1/3 HP) about 800 W running, 1,300 W starting.
Fridge + 4 LED bulbs for 5 hours + router + 2 phones uses about 2,300 Wh a day; with losses and buffer that is about 3,300 Wh for one day.
Most portable power stations output 120 V only; central AC, electric dryers, ovens and many well pumps run on 240 V.
Connecting a power station to home wiring requires a proper transfer switch or inlet installed by a licensed electrician; never backfeed through an outlet.
Expandable systems accept extra battery packs; adding solar recharges during multi-day outages.
Battery power stations make no fumes and can be used indoors, unlike gas generators.
Plan essentials first: food cold, communication, light, medical devices, flood protection.
